questions.question: What is the lesson's core production invariant?
options: Release the caption with the highest decoder confidence.
Release every caption that contains all requested keywords.
Support every released claim with permitted evidence and make it useful for the declared task.
Use the same caption for accessibility, search, and editorial workflows.
questions.explanation: Decoder preference and task usefulness are separate from evidence. A release needs both permitted support for its claims and a purpose-specific contract.

questions.question: Why can a lexical constraint make a caption less trustworthy?
options: It can force a required word even when the image does not support the corresponding claim.
It always changes beam search into greedy decoding.
It removes every visual token from the encoder.
It guarantees that the decoder returns an empty string.
questions.explanation: A lexical constraint controls emitted language, not visual truth. Grounding must still validate the claim associated with the required token or phrase.

questions.question: A synthetic evaluation set has 8 cases, and 3 contain at least one unsupported claim. What is the hallucination-case rate?
questions.explanation: The case rate is 3 / 8 = 0.375, or 37.5%. It is distinct from the total number of unsupported claims.

questions.question: Which evaluation pairing most directly separates consensus wording from unsupported-object failures?
options: CIDEr for reference consensus and CHAIR for hallucinated object mentions.
Latency for consensus and throughput for object correctness.
Beam width for consensus and temperature for object correctness.
OCR confidence for consensus and token count for object correctness.
questions.explanation: CIDEr compares a candidate with human reference consensus, while CHAIR was designed to identify object mentions absent from ground-truth objects.

questions.question: Overall coverage is 90.9%, but the best slice covers 100% of required facts and the low-light slice covers 57.1%. What should a 15-point maximum slice-gap gate do?
options: Pass because overall coverage exceeds 90%.
Pass because no unsupported claim was generated.
Block because the 42.9-point slice gap exceeds the declared limit.
Remove the low-light cases and recompute the average.
questions.explanation: The gap is 100 - 57.1 = 42.9 percentage points. A required slice gate cannot be averaged away by stronger common cases.

questions.question: What does a decoder confidence value establish?
options: That every object in the sentence is present in the image.
The model's preference under its conditioning and scoring setup, not independent factual support.
That human reviewers will find the caption useful.
That the caption satisfies every safety policy.
questions.explanation: Decoder confidence ranks language under the model. Claim-level evidence, task policy, and human usefulness are separate signals.

questions.question: Why should alt-text evaluation include the image's page context and purpose?
options: The same pixels can need different essential information depending on what the image does in the page.
Page context makes visual grounding unnecessary.
Decorative images always need a detailed scene description.
Context converts every caption into structured metadata.
questions.explanation: W3C guidance ties a text alternative to the image's purpose and context. A caption can be visually accurate yet still omit the information the user needs.
